capabilities.question: Does a vanilla item the off-hand normally accepts -- a shield -- stay there when a script puts it in?
capabilities.decides:
Nothing on its own, and that is the point. This is the CONTROL for every other row in this file: it is the one that is SUPPOSED to work.
If it does not stay, the apparatus is broken -- the write never landed, or the read is looking at the wrong slot, or there was no player there at all -- and every negative in this file is measuring the probe rather than the game. Without it, a probe that had silently stopped writing anything would report exactly the same confident row of NOs as one working perfectly, and a manifest people design around would be built on it.

capabilities.question: Does `setEquipment(Offhand, ...)` succeed for an item the slot would not normally take?
capabilities.decides: Whether the API refuses outright. Separating this from whether the item STAYS is the whole point -- a refusal and an ejection look identical a moment later, and they point at different workarounds.
capabilities.evidence: setEquipment succeeded and the slot read back correctly

capabilities.question: Is a script-placed arbitrary vanilla item still in the off-hand a few seconds later?

capabilities.note: Imported from composable-portals docs/CAPABILITIES.md (P9). Closes an attractive idea: had script-placed items stuck, the off-hand would have given free in-world rendering of an arbitrary item with no attachable work at all.

capabilities.question: When the client ejects a script-placed item from the off-hand, does the item still exist?
capabilities.decides: Whether writing to the off-hand is SAFE TO ATTEMPT AT ALL. Everything else in this file is about whether a trick works; this is about what it costs when it does not. An ejection that returns the item to the inventory or drops it on the floor is a failed effect. An ejection that destroys it is a pack eating a player's diamonds, and no amount of graceful degradation elsewhere makes that acceptable.

capabilities.question: Does `max_durability` report back exactly what was declared, all the way up to 32767?
capabilities.decides: How many bits a packed-durability design has to work with. Vanilla's own ceiling is 2031 (netherite), so anything above that is undocumented territory, and the difference between ~6 usable bits and ~15 is the difference between a layout that fits and one that does not.
capabilities.evidence: everything up to and including 32767 reports back exactly what was declared
capabilities.note: Imported from composable-portals docs/CAPABILITIES.md (P1), headless smoke job, PR #36 run 30516360479. Vanilla's own ceiling is 2031 (netherite), so everything above that was undocumented territory. 15 usable bits.

capabilities.question: Above the ceiling, does `max_durability` wrap negative rather than clamping?
capabilities.decides: Whether an over-large computed code has a safe failure mode. A clamp degrades to the maximum and stays sane; a wrap goes negative and nonsensical while the item still loads. If it wraps, whatever builds a packed value has to assert its own range, because nothing else will.
capabilities.evidence: two's-complement int16 wraparound, and the item still loads
capabilities.note: Imported from composable-portals docs/CAPABILITIES.md (P1). A clamp has a safe failure mode and a wrap does not: an over-large value does not degrade to the maximum, it becomes negative and nonsensical, and the item still loads. Whatever computes a packed code must assert its own range.

capabilities.question: What downward velocity does a vanilla falling block reach after a fixed number of ticks?
capabilities.decides: Whether a mechanic can predict where a falling block will be, rather than watching it. It is also the control for every other row in this file: if this number moves, the engine's integration changed and nothing else measured here can be compared across that boundary.

capabilities.question: How far above a falling anvil can a block vacate its path and still be clear when the anvil arrives?
capabilities.decides: The tightest a pass-under mechanic can be built before it becomes unreliable. Something has to move out of the way, moving takes time, and this is how much room that time costs. It is a technical problem asking to be optimised into a reference implementation, and the number it optimises to is only meaningful if somebody is watching whether it moves.

capabilities.question: How far does an item given a fixed impulse travel before coming to rest on flat ground?
capabilities.decides: Whether a mechanic that throws something can predict where it lands. Recorded not because throw distance is interesting in itself, but because anything built on top of it inherits the drag, the friction and the integration underneath it -- and a design tuned to the old numbers fails in a way that looks like a bug in the design rather than a change in the game.

capabilities.question: How far does one unit of `applyKnockback` actually move a player?
capabilities.decides: Whether any momentum design can be written at all. `applyKnockback` is the only way to impose a velocity on a player -- `applyImpulse` refuses them outright -- and its unit is undocumented, so every use of it anywhere is a constant somebody tuned by hand until it looked right.

capabilities.question: How far does one unit of `applyKnockback` move an ordinary entity?
capabilities.decides: Whether one momentum constant covers everything a mechanic might move, or whether players and everything else need separate numbers. A design that pushes both through the same call and assumes the same result is resting on a proposition nobody has checked.

capabilities.question: Does an unrecognised Molang query resolve to 0 rather than erroring?
capabilities.decides: How every other probe in this file has to be read. If an unknown query silently yields 0, then a controller indexing a texture array with a dead query still draws -- it draws index 0. So index 0 is the signal for "this query is blind", and no probe expectation may land on index 0 except the one that expects zero anyway. Getting this backwards makes every rendering measurement unreadable.
capabilities.established_by: Read off the engine's behaviour across several controller failures. An unresolvable query for an ENTITY property additionally fails the whole render controller silently, which is a different and worse failure -- four sessions were lost to it before the query was found to be `query.property` rather than `query.actor_property`.

capabilities.question: Does Molang's float arithmetic stay exact across a bit-packed integer layout?
capabilities.decides: Whether `math.floor` and `math.mod` can safely unpack a value carried in durability or any other numeric channel.
capabilities.established_by: Molang is float-based; integers stay exact well past 2^24, which is far above any packed layout worth designing. Use power-of-two bases for readability.

capabilities.question: Does a custom item render an attachable at all?
capabilities.decides: Whether in-world rendering of a custom held item is possible in any form. The bisect floor for everything else in this file: a rig that stays dark cannot say whether the queries are blind or whether attachables simply do not work on custom items, and without this row underneath it, no result above is readable.
capabilities.evidence: third person showed it plainly as a cube; first person was filled with magenta because the hand pivot is essentially at the camera
capabilities.note: Imported from composable-portals docs/CAPABILITIES.md (P3a). The most consequential row in the battery was the negative, and it did not happen. The failure that would have killed the route was INVISIBLE — magenta everywhere is not invisible, and Bedrock's own missing-texture is a checker rather than a solid field, so the two were distinguishable.

capabilities.question: Can a render controller on an attachable read the durability of the item it draws?
capabilities.decides: The largest single consequence in this battery. If yes, ONE item type renders every configuration in the hand and hundreds of baked sprites go away. If no, the item looks identical in every configuration and its state has to live in its NAME and its DURABILITY BAR, which are the only two per-stack visuals left.
capabilities.evidence: two items differing only in damage (5 and 6) drew identically, with the control bone BLUE on both
capabilities.note: Imported from composable-portals docs/CAPABILITIES.md (P3b/P4). Read differentially after two earlier attempts could not be graded: an absolute reading was structurally ambiguous, because with max_durability 2048 an undamaged item shows the same colours as a blind query. All three durability queries resolve to 0 — the expression resolves, it just never sees an item. Consequence: a render controller cannot be told which item it is drawing, so every distinguishable configuration needs its own item type, and per-stack state has to live in the NAME and the DURABILITY BAR.

capabilities.question: Does an attachable with no `animations` and no `scripts.animate` render at the player model's own origin?
capabilities.decides: Whether "it appeared on my back" is a property of attachables or a property of our geometry offsets. The answer changes whether a hand pose needs work or just needs coordinates.
capabilities.established_by: Read directly out of the attachable JSON we emit: it declares only `materials`, `textures`, `geometry` and `render_controllers`. With nothing switching poses, the model renders in the player model's coordinate space at its origin and stays there in both first and third person. Confirmed against play reports of the probe appearing behind the player, which is where its authored offset puts it.
